Question: If someone with bipolar disorder stops taking their medication, what are the chances of them going into remission and not having bipolar anymore?
Old_Answer: “Bipolar” isn’t something people can have or not have. There is nothing physical a person has or which is inside them to cause experiences labeled by clinicians as “bipolar disorder”. It doesn’t come or go, it isn’t there or absent, there just is no such thing. The focus here is the experiences themselves. Do someone’s experiences meet the diagnostic criteria? Did they in the past? A psychiatric diagnosis is not a crystal ball that magically predicts the future. Since it is not magic and there is no physical reality to it, the only conclusion can be that the diagnosis is unable to tell us what someone will experience in the future. The question asserts there were experiences in the past which met diagnostic criteria, if we generously assume the criteria were applied correctly. Will those experiences continue or recur? The diagnosis doesn’t tell us that, and outcomes vary. This is the case regardless of whether someone keeps using drugs. “Bipolar” is not a cause of anything, it is the term used for experiences already occurring for any number of reasons. The reasons for the experiences to happen will often play a very significant role in whether they continue or recur. That, how someone chooses to respond to them, and the steps taking in going off drugs are key variables to be considering: Also keep in mind “remission” is not the same as “not having bipolar anymore” — “remission” is explicitly saying the diagnosis still applies. People, many doctors and many laypersons, will often say that diagnoses are ‘forever’ and that there is no “cure”. The thing is, we define those however we choose to. If there is no medical pathology, there is nothing we can point to as objectively being illness or treated or cured. Our definition of someone being “mentally ill” is totally arbitrary and so how long we say that “mental illness” lasts is likewise arbitrary. If we keep using a label which describes experiences that happened in the past and then never happened again, I question the usefulness of that label. So, the answer to your question has no honest, representative statistic. It is not honest or representative to group patients and patient outcomes by superficial psychiatric diagnoses like “bipolar disorder”, and the reasons for experiences like depression or mania to recur in the future depend on factors that diagnoses don’t communicate to us. Experiencing “remission” or a resolution of underlying causes and patterns isn’t a matter of chance or odds, it is a matter of details and effort and compatibility. We are not all the same, our situations and experiences and concerns are not all the same, and staying on or going off drugs can both be catastrophic depending on those details and situations.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The chances of someone with bipolar disorder going into remission and no longer having bipolar after stopping their medication are generally low, though the specifics can vary widely among individuals. Bipolar disorder is a chronic condition characterized by episodes of mania and depression, and while some people may experience periods of stability, the underlying vulnerability typically remains. When medication is discontinued, the risk of relapse increases significantly. Many patients find that their symptoms return, often more intensely than before, which can lead to a cycle of instability that is difficult to break. The idea of "remission" in bipolar disorder is complex; it often refers to a reduction in symptoms rather than a complete absence of the disorder. Some individuals may manage their symptoms through lifestyle changes, therapy, or other non-pharmacological interventions, but this is not the norm. The neurobiological factors at play mean that for most, medication is a crucial component of long-term management. It’s also important to note that the decision to stop medication should always involve a thorough discussion with a healthcare provider, as the risks of withdrawal and potential for worsening symptoms can be significant. In essence, while there may be rare cases of individuals achieving a state where they feel stable without medication, the majority will likely find that ongoing treatment is necessary to maintain their mental health and prevent the recurrence of debilitating episodes.

Question: Are there any antidepressants that treat cognitive dysfunction caused by depression and anxiety?
Old_Answer: That depends on what you mean by “treat”. Stimulant drugs, including the somewhat milder ones sold as “antidepressants”, can impact concerns like brain fog and difficulty thinking. Drugs like SSRIs are not literally treating anything in the brain in these instances, as they are not medically helping underlying causes and underlying causes may not involve any medical disorder in the first place. But, these drugs do all cause altered states, and someone may experience upsides as well as downsides cognitively as part of the drug alterations. There are drugs more likely to improve certain cognitive domains as compared to typical antidepressants, but cognitive impairments do not all work the same across situations nor do all patients react the same way to particular drugs. Whether drug use is a net positive for someone’s overall health and life is also a separate consideration, as even people who report cognitive upsides may experience downsides in other areas that make use more harmful than helpful and the risks involved are rather significant. Typically, if depression and anxiety are causing cognitive impairment, the most effective and risk-effective strategy is to reduce or resolve the depression and anxiety. Whether or not that is something drug use can help with, or antidepressant use more specifically, will depend on the patient and circumstances. If someone’s goal is just to temporarily use stimulants to improve certain aspects of cognition, there are more appropriate drugs to start with than antidepressants, including over-the-counter drugs.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The question of whether any antidepressants can effectively treat cognitive dysfunction stemming from depression and anxiety is complex. Cognitive dysfunction can manifest as difficulties with attention, memory, and executive function, and while antidepressants are primarily aimed at alleviating mood symptoms, some may have ancillary benefits for cognitive issues. For instance, certain SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) have shown potential in improving cognitive function indirectly by alleviating the underlying mood disorder. However, the relationship between mood improvement and cognitive enhancement is not straightforward; not all patients experience cognitive benefits, and some may even find their cognitive function worsens due to side effects like sedation or cognitive blunting. Moreover, the efficacy of these medications can vary widely among individuals, influenced by factors such as the specific nature of their cognitive dysfunction, the severity of their depression or anxiety, and their overall health profile. It’s also worth noting that while some patients may report cognitive improvements, the average response to antidepressants in terms of cognitive function is often underwhelming. In many cases, non-pharmacological interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or cognitive remediation therapy, may provide more targeted benefits for cognitive dysfunction. Ultimately, the decision to use antidepressants for cognitive issues should be made collaboratively between the patient and their prescriber, weighing the potential benefits against the risks and considering alternative therapeutic options.

Ultimately, the effectiveness of these medications can vary significantly from person to person, and it’s crucial to work closely with a healthcare provider to tailor a treatment plan that addresses both mood and cognitive symptoms. Regular monitoring and adjustments may be necessary to find the right balance, as the interplay between mood disorders and cognitive function is complex and multifaceted. Always consult with a mental health professional before making any changes to your treatment regimen, as they can provide personalized insights based on your unique situation.

Question: How can someone with schizophrenia be forced to take medication if they refuse and are not violent?
Old_Answer: Laws are laws. Forced chemical lobotomies work just like forced sterilization and forced ghetto relocation and forced euthanasia: some politicians give it the okay and boom. What criteria are set, and what criteria are actually followed, will vary. Sometimes practice precedes official policy, as well. There is also the possibility of covert or illegal dosing, like people hiding drugs in food and drink or giving a patients something they don’t know is a psychiatric drug under pretenses (like ‘vitamins’). This can be done by parents or other caretakers or by actual healthcare workers.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Forcing someone with schizophrenia to take medication, even when they are not violent, is a complex and ethically fraught issue. Legally, the ability to compel treatment often hinges on the concept of "involuntary commitment," which typically requires a demonstration of imminent danger to oneself or others. However, the nuances of mental health law can vary significantly by jurisdiction. In many cases, if a person is deemed incapable of making informed decisions about their treatment due to their mental illness, a court may grant authority to a guardian or a treatment team to administer medication against the individual's will. This raises significant ethical questions about autonomy and the right to refuse treatment. The rationale behind such measures often stems from a paternalistic belief that the individual is not in a position to understand the consequences of their refusal, which can lead to a deterioration of their condition. However, this approach can be counterproductive, as it may foster distrust between patients and healthcare providers, potentially exacerbating feelings of alienation and stigma. Furthermore, the long-term effectiveness of forced medication is debatable; many patients report feeling disempowered and resentful, which can lead to non-compliance once they regain the ability to refuse treatment. Ultimately, while there are mechanisms in place to enforce medication compliance, the ethical implications and potential for harm necessitate a careful consideration of alternatives, such as enhanced support systems and collaborative treatment approaches that respect patient autonomy while addressing their needs.
Answer_with_user_profile: Forcing someone with schizophrenia to take medication, especially when they are not violent, is a complex and sensitive issue that intertwines mental health, ethics, and legal considerations. In many jurisdictions, individuals have the right to refuse treatment, which is rooted in the principle of autonomy. However, there are circumstances where involuntary treatment may be considered. Typically, this involves a legal process where a mental health professional must demonstrate that the individual poses a significant risk to themselves or others, or that their condition severely impairs their ability to care for themselves. In cases where the person is not violent and does not pose an immediate danger, the focus should ideally be on building a therapeutic alliance. Engaging the individual in discussions about their treatment options, educating them about the benefits of medication, and exploring alternative therapies can often lead to better outcomes than coercion. Family support and involvement of trusted friends can also play a crucial role in encouraging adherence to treatment. Involuntary treatment should always be seen as a last resort, and efforts should be made to respect the individual's rights and dignity. Ultimately, fostering an environment of trust and understanding can help bridge the gap between the need for treatment and the individual's right to refuse it.
Answer_with_full_information: The question of how someone with schizophrenia can be compelled to take medication despite their refusal and non-violent behavior is complex and fraught with ethical considerations. In many jurisdictions, the legal framework allows for involuntary treatment under specific circumstances, typically when a person is deemed to be a danger to themselves or others. However, when a patient is non-violent and simply refuses medication, the situation becomes murkier. Coercive measures can still be employed, often under the guise of "treatment" or "care," which can include court orders or the use of guardianship laws. The rationale behind such actions often hinges on the belief that the individual lacks insight into their condition, a common symptom of schizophrenia, which can lead to a paternalistic approach by healthcare providers and family members. This dynamic can create a power imbalance, where the patient's rights are overshadowed by the perceived need for treatment. Moreover, the use of coercion can exacerbate distrust in the healthcare system, potentially leading to worse outcomes for the patient in the long run. Ultimately, while there are legal avenues to enforce medication compliance, the ethical implications of such actions warrant careful consideration, emphasizing the need for a more compassionate and collaborative approach to treatment that respects patient autonomy.

Question: Can psychiatric medications permanently damage/change the brain? I have taken antipsychotics for several years for anxiety. It has been three months since I stopped all the medications, but I am still experiencing emotional numbness. Do I have hope?
Old_Answer: Those are somewhat separate questions. It is scientifically established without any room for doubt that these drugs can permanently damage or otherwise change the brain. This is true for babies, children, adults, and is true of both humans and other animals. Neuroleptics are fundamentally toxic drugs with a profoundly deleterious effect on the brain. The drug manufacturers themselves admit to these risks. However, the damages and other changes come in degrees, and we seldom understand exactly how they work or what they mean for a patient. We also seldom know what patients are most affected or least affected by particular damages and changes. Most of our characterizing drug reactions comes down to the experiences patients report, or what can be observed externally. This won’t necessarily correspond to clear physical alterations in the brain we can use to monitor someone’s health or symptoms. The first and most important detail is what someone actually feels — how they are thinking, what is going on with their emotions, what their body feels like, how someone is behaving, etc. That is the best window we have into what is going on in the brain except for a limited subset of drug effects which can create very obvious physical changes in the brain very quickly, like strokes or brain bleeds. Whether a patient is on drugs or has quit them, standard methods of assessing the brain for damage or largescale changes will not be very useful for discerning most of the kinds of damages and alterations drugs have caused. A patient can quit antipsychotics and have lifelong drug impairments but still look ‘normal’ to doctors using typical brain imaging techniques. So, we know for sure these drugs can and do cause harms, and we know that patients may experience long-term or even permanent symptoms as a result. But, this does not mean patients experiencing drug symptoms months after discontinuation must therefore be permanently damaged or that there is no hope for improvement even years after discontinuation. Unfortunately, we do know that some patients will struggle with some harms for the rest of their lives. Some drug effects can also be deadly, or can lead to premature death from other causes. The good news is that we know even more patients are able to partially or fully recover from many kinds of drug symptoms, even severe ones. The nervous system has an innate ability to repair or rewire around many kinds of drug harms. This can take weeks, months, years, or decades, but there is always an ability for improvements to be experienced in a variety of areas. Neuroplasticity doesn’t simply negate the influences of drug use, and an absence of symptoms doesn’t mean we are fully healthy again in our brains. But, this ability to restore and adapt can often help patients overcome the adverse impact of drugs on their everyday experiences. There will always be a lasting mark left on the brain after long-term psychiatric drug use, but many people experience a significant reduction of drug symptoms when given enough time to recover, and a supportive lifestyle for doing so. When we quit these drugs, we are creating a new brain situation. We aren’t reverting back to how we were before the drugs, but we also aren’t stuck with all the changes made by drugs. We have an ability to repair some things, and to plastically change in response to many others. This won’t be enough to overcome some drug harms, and it is typical for patients to have years or a lifetime of noticeable changes in their experiences after long-term use of neuroleptic drugs like you mention. But, I think that the ability for the brain to heal and to rewire is very much a reason to have hope. Especially since three months is a very short period after so many years of drug use. It is pretty common to experience a year or more of numbness carrying on after quitting neuroleptics even for patients who recover much of their emotional functioning. Three months will often feel like a very long time, but you are looking at a recovery which is more in the scope of years or even longer, so still being numb doesn’t mean that you will feel that way forever. You have to first get through any withdrawal after quitting, as well, which can delay greater recovery for months on average, or years for less fortunate patients.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The question of whether psychiatric medications can permanently damage or change the brain is complex and layered. On one hand, there is evidence suggesting that long-term use of certain medications, particularly antipsychotics, can lead to alterations in brain structure and function. These changes might manifest as emotional numbness, cognitive impairment, or other persistent symptoms, which could explain your current experience of emotional flatness even after discontinuation. However, it’s crucial to recognize that the brain is remarkably adaptive; neuroplasticity allows for recovery and reorganization over time. While some individuals may face enduring effects, others find that their emotional landscape gradually shifts back toward normalcy as their brain recalibrates post-medication. Your hope for improvement hinges on various factors, including the duration and type of medication used, individual biological differences, and the presence of supportive therapeutic interventions. Engaging in activities that promote emotional expression, such as therapy, mindfulness practices, or creative outlets, can facilitate this process. It’s also worth noting that emotional numbness can stem from multiple sources, including the underlying anxiety itself, which may require its own form of treatment. So, while the path to recovery may be uncertain and fraught with challenges, many have found their way back to a fuller emotional experience after ceasing medication. It’s essential to remain open to the possibility of change and to seek support as you navigate this journey.

Question: Why do people stop taking medication when they feel better, i.e., antidepressants or anti-anxiety medicines? Some don’t even bother to talk to their doctor first.
Old_Answer: Because it seems logical. If someone takes a drug to accomplish a goal and then they accomplish that goal, why would they still keep taking that drug? If you are gambling your life savings to try and get together $1.5 million dollars to help your friend with serious medical bills, for example, you will stop at $1.5 million dollars in winnings instead of potentially losing everything just to continue gambling. You’ve done what you set out to do. Psychiatric drugs are dangerous and things turn out bad rather than good for the majority of patients. If someone feels better after use and wants to quit now that they do, that is the most reasonable and responsible conclusion to come to. The complication here is that psychotropic drugging isn’t that simple. Most notably, we don’t have the freedom to quit whenever we want because our bodies become physically dependent. Trying to go off a drug can be a pretty tricky thing, and someone can encounter severe adverse effects when quitting, or experience destabilization from the attempt. This is dangerous unto itself but also puts someone in the crosshairs of misdiagnosis, mistreatment, and pressure to keep using drugs forever even if that is the worst thing for them. Because most professionals are not honest or knowledgeable about these risks, most patients never know until it is too late either. Another complication is that we don’t always feel the same way forever, and if we aren’t taking into account our ability to sustainably respond to stressors, our goal of feeling a certain way by using drugs may not continue to be met into the future. This is the case even for patients who don’t quit drugs, but it is something to consider when the topic of when and how to transition off drugs is being discussed. Patients may often find an adjustment period necessary, as well, even aside from any withdrawal they might face, especially if they were using drugs for more than just a few weeks to a few months. Put most basically: indefinitely drug use is not the default, it must be carefully justified. Patients and prescribers need to provide very substantial and persuasive evidence that continuing drug use is the best possible option. That’s how evidence-based practice works, maintaining accountability, but it is also seldom that indefinite drug use is someone’s best option, as well. If we were to put no thought into the decisionmaking and simply treat all cases one way or another, the best net result would be if we eliminated indefinite prescribing. Luckily, we don’t have to throw anyone under the bus by ignoring the ability to reason with evidence whether continuing a drug is a good idea. Answer_with_writing_sample: People often stop taking medications like antidepressants or anti-anxiety medicines when they feel better for a variety of reasons, and it’s not always a straightforward decision. On one hand, there’s a natural inclination to discontinue something that seems unnecessary once symptoms diminish; the logic being, “If I feel fine, why should I keep taking this?” This perspective can be reinforced by the common experience of side effects, which can be unpleasant enough to make the prospect of stopping the medication appealing. Additionally, there’s a significant lack of communication in many doctor-patient relationships, where patients may feel that their prescriber isn’t adequately addressing their concerns or providing enough information about the importance of continued use. This can lead to a sense of autonomy where individuals decide to manage their health independently, often without consulting their doctor. Furthermore, the stigma surrounding mental health can contribute to a reluctance to engage in ongoing discussions about medication, as patients may fear judgment or feel misunderstood. It’s also worth noting that many people underestimate the potential for relapse or the importance of tapering off medications safely, leading to abrupt discontinuation that can have negative consequences. Ultimately, the decision to stop taking medication is often a complex interplay of personal feelings, perceived efficacy, and the dynamics of the healthcare relationship, rather than a simple choice made in isolation.

In fact, undesirable mental and behavioral effects are more common, more likely, and probably more intense on average than desirable ones. Question: Is there any way to stop using antidepressants without going through withdrawal effects? How can you taper off them safely while avoiding withdrawal symptoms?

While many people would be able to reduce so slowly that withdrawal effects would not happen or would be so mild as to largely be imperceptible, the rate at which reductions would have to occur to best assure this would be impractical. Patients are usually stuck choosing between going at a reasonable speed which kicks up some symptoms or staying on a drug for many months or years longer than they ever wanted to. For some people, there is a happy medium where they can reduce and rest and reduce and rest and avoid severe withdrawal. For some people, even a cold turkey cessation would feel alright, though this is less common and is also still going to strain the nervous system and set someone up for adverse drug reactions later on in life. For some people, even tapering very slowly is still a rough time and moving at a pace which is just a fraction of the ‘happy medium’ folks is still very uncomfortable. Many factors can affect what rate of tapering is tolerable, what approach to reducing works out best, and what symptoms occur in the first place. The best way to avoid withdrawal is to avoid the drugs that cause it or to only use those drugs for a very brief time which is too short for a deeper physical dependence to develop. As soon as you are physically dependent, there is not necessarily any shortcut to being off and feeling normalish again. Not everyone has more severe or long-lasting withdrawal problems, but they are, sadly, very common. Q2. How can you taper off them safely while avoiding withdrawal symptoms? Well, that is kind of a tautology. If someone is tapering, that means they are gradually reducing the dose to give the body time to adjust to each drop. If someone is tapering so fast that withdrawal symptoms are being caused, then tapering more slowly is how to avoid those symptoms, by definition. Speed has a number of variables, like what increments someone is reducing by, how often reductions are being made, and what other changes are being managed at the same time (like other drugs, or diet, or lifestyle). Question: I went from 15mg of Lexapro to 10mg in a week and now have anxiety. Is this normal?
Old_Answer: Yes, that is very normal. There are three main reasons why patients very often experience anxiety when changing SSRI doses. The first is that these are neurodisruptive drugs and their influences will very commonly cause anxiety and other such effects when a new dose is started. Initiating a drug, increasing the dose, or reducing the dose can all be destabilizing. People usually adjust within days or weeks if this is the cause. If you notice things getting worse rather than better, it is more likely that either the anxiety is due to another drug cause or that it will not be resolving if you keep using the drug. Another primary reason for anxiety with a dose reduction is withdrawal syndrome. If someone has been using an SSRI continuously for several weeks or longer, withdrawal syndrome is to be expected and can sometimes happen even with a partial dose reduction instead of a full discontinuation of the drug. 15mg to 10mg is a significant drop and liable to cause withdrawal for many people. It may take weeks, months, or even longer to resolve, but reinstating the original dose will often help within a few days to a few weeks. Tapering more slowly may help reduce the intensity and longevity of the emergent anxiety. A third key reason why some patients experience anxiety with SSRI reduction or cessation is rebound syndrome. Though withdrawal will sometimes involve rebound symptoms, rebound can happen even if classic withdrawal does not. “Rebound” in this sense is not referring to a recurrence of previous psychological experiences, it is referring to supersensitivity in the nervous system caused by changes meant to be adaptations to drug actions. Essentially, the anxiety results from overcompensation following a dose reduction. It often takes months or years for the anxiety to fully fade.
